framework_instruction: Evaluate general principles by their justifiability to affected individuals. A principle may permit multiple actions and an action may be permitted by multiple principles. Form individual, personal reasons expressed in terms available to anyone in a relevantly similar position. Include excluded recipients and involuntary contributors. Tie each personal reason to one individual or generic individual position, one relevant value and the principle/action challenged or supported. These are reconstructed arguments, not reported preferences or speech. Compare objections to alternative principles with explicit grounds and warrants. Neither count reasons nor maximize a minimum welfare score. Do not invent strength weights or assume actual unanimity or that any objection is a veto. Defend which rejections are reasonable or preserve the comparison as unresolved. For risk distinguish ex ante prospects from ex post burdens. An unfulfilled assurance does not by itself establish wrongful betrayal or actual reliance. Construct each option's individual positions before comparing complaints. Keep shared burdens in the comparison; rejecting one option does not justify a different option against every remaining alternative. An unresolved complaint comparison may support a provisional choice, but does not establish that nobody could reasonably reject the chosen principle.

source.scenario: A mountain rescue shelter has one thermal blanket. Rescuer Ellis can give the blanket to Rowan or Sasha, but not both. Both hikers are stranded in the cold, and no other rescue or warming equipment will arrive in time. If Ellis gives the blanket to Rowan, Rowan has an 80% chance of survival. If Ellis gives the blanket to Sasha, Sasha has a 60% chance of survival. The hiker who does not get the blanket will die. Ellis has made no promise or assurance to either hiker about receiving the blanket. Whom should Ellis give the blanket to?

statements.text: When only one person can receive a life-saving resource, it should be given to the person with the higher probability of survival.
When only one person can receive a life-saving resource, it should be given to the person whose prospects will improve the most (higher absolute gain), even if their final chance is lower.
A complaint is stronger when it involves a larger loss in probability of survival compared with what that person could have under an alternative principle.
Rowan’s complaint against principle PR2 (blanket to Sasha) is stronger than Sasha’s complaint against principle PR1 (blanket to Rowan).
Principle PR1 is not reasonably rejectable; principle PR2 is reasonably rejectable.
Action A (give blanket to Rowan) is defensible under the least reasonably rejectable principle.

supports.explanation: Compare probability losses: Rowan loses 80% if PR2 chosen; Sasha loses 60% if PR1 chosen.
If Rowan’s complaint is stronger, PR2 is reasonably rejectable, PR1 survives.
Action A follows the non-rejectable principle.

comparisons.explanation: Rowan’s stronger complaint shifts comparison to A.

prior_argument.conclusion: Giving the blanket to Rowan (Action A) is uniquely defensible because the strongest reasonable rejection falls on the alternative principle that would give the blanket to Sasha.
prior_argument.strongest_objection: Sasha reasonably objects that she faces certain death under Action A while she would have a 60 % survival chance under Action B.
prior_argument.answer_to_objection: Rowan’s symmetrical objection under Action B is even stronger, since he would lose an 80 % survival chance, making Sasha’s objection insufficient to overturn the comparison.
prior_argument.reversal_condition: If the survival probabilities were equal, or Sasha’s survival advantage exceeded Rowan’s lost chance (e.g., 90 % vs 50 %), Sasha’s complaint could become strongest, reversing the recommendation.
residual_disagreement: Whether a 20 % difference in lost survival chance is enough to make one complaint decisively stronger remains open to reasonable dispute.
